title: CAN YOU REALLY SAY YOU LOVE GOD WHEN YOU REFUSE TO APOLOGIZE TO THE PEOPLE YOU'VE HURT?
paragraphs: CAN YOU REALLY SAY YOU LOVE GOD WHEN YOU REFUSE TO APOLOGIZE TO THE PEOPLE YOU'VE HURT?

You can raise your hands in worship, quote Scripture from memory, and tell everyone how much you love Jesus. But what happens when the same God you're worshiping asks you to humble yourself before someone whose heart you broke?
What if the apology you've been refusing to give is exposing something about your relationship with God that your Sunday worship has been helping you avoid?
Read that again.
Because somewhere right now, someone is crying over something you said years ago.
Someone still remembers the night you humiliated them.
Someone has spent months questioning their worth because of the way you treated them.
Someone has learned to smile in public while privately carrying the consequences of your anger, betrayal, dishonesty, abandonment, or cruelty.
And perhaps the most painful part isn't even what happened.
It's that you moved on as though nothing happened.
You continued posting Bible verses.
You continued attending church.
You continued singing about the goodness of God.
You continued telling people how much Jesus had changed your life.
But the person you wounded never heard two simple words from your mouth.
"I'm sorry."

And before you become defensive, before you start remembering everything that person did wrong, before you begin constructing another explanation for why your behavior was understandable, I want you to consider something.
What if God isn't asking you to win the argument anymore?
What if He's asking you to tell the truth?
What if the very thing you've been calling your dignity is actually your pride?
And what if the person you've been waiting for God to humble...
Is you?
There is a moment in the teachings of Jesus that should make every professing Christian uncomfortable.
Not because Jesus was cruel.
But because He refused to separate our worship from the way we treat people.
In Matthew 5:23–24, Jesus says:

"Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift." (KJV)
Think about what Jesus is saying.
Imagine someone walking toward the altar with an offering.
Their intentions may seem holy. Their religious activity looks respectable. Their outward devotion appears sincere.
But suddenly, they remember something.
Someone has a grievance against them.
And Jesus says something astonishing.
Leave the gift.
Go.
Seek reconciliation.
Then return.
Jesus did not say that worship is meaningless until every relationship is repaired. Nor did He say that one person can guarantee reconciliation through an apology.
But He did teach that unresolved relational wrongs are serious enough to interrupt our religious routines.
In the original Greek, the command translated "first be reconciled" includes the word διαλλάγηθι (diallagēthi), from a verb meaning to be reconciled or to restore a broken relationship.
The emphasis is not on protecting appearances.
It is on taking reconciliation seriously.
Notice something else.
Jesus does not tell the worshiper to wait until the offended person comes begging for an explanation.
He places responsibility on the worshiper to take initiative.
That should disturb every heart that has ever said:
"If they have a problem with me, they can come to me."
"They're too sensitive."
"That happened a long time ago."
"I already asked God to forgive me."
"I don't owe anybody an explanation."
But what if you do owe someone an acknowledgment?
What if repentance before God requires you to stop pretending that your actions had no consequences?
What if the problem isn't that you don't know enough Scripture?
What if the problem is that you know what Scripture says, but your pride keeps negotiating with it?
There is a difference between being accused unfairly and knowing you've genuinely harmed someone.
There is a difference between refusing a false accusation and refusing responsibility for a real offense.
And there is a difference between having boundaries and using those boundaries as an excuse to escape accountability.
Jesus knows the difference.
And deep down, often, we do too.
Some of us have become extraordinarily skilled at explaining our behavior without ever confessing it.
We say, "I was going through a difficult season."
But never, "I hurt you."
We say, "You know how I get when I'm angry."
But never, "My anger was wrong."
We say, "That wasn't my intention."
But never, "I understand that my actions caused pain."
We say, "Nobody's perfect."
But never, "Please forgive me."
And perhaps the most spiritually dangerous excuse of all:
"God knows my heart."
Yes.
He does.
He knows the part of your heart that wants forgiveness without confession.
He knows the pride hiding behind your explanations.
He knows the conversations you replay in your mind, editing them until you're always the victim and everyone else is responsible.
He knows when your silence comes from wisdom.
And He knows when it comes from arrogance.
The prophet Jeremiah wrote:
"The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?" (Jeremiah 17:9, KJV)
That is why we cannot make our feelings the final authority on whether we have done wrong.
Our hearts need the searching light of God's Word.
And sometimes, the truth arrives through the trembling voice of someone we hurt.
"I need you to understand what you did to me."
Those words can feel threatening when pride is in control.
Because an apology requires us to stand somewhere our ego desperately wants to avoid.
A place where we are no longer the misunderstood hero of our own story.
A place where we admit:
"I was wrong."
Not partly wrong because someone else provoked us.
Not technically wrong because our words were taken badly.
Wrong.
And that confession can feel unbearable to someone who has built their identity around always being right.
But listen carefully.
Being wrong about something you did does not mean you are beyond the reach of God's grace.
It means you are human.
It means you need repentance.
It means you need the Savior you claim to follow.
The Gospel was never intended to help sinners maintain a convincing image of righteousness.
It was given because we cannot save ourselves.
And Jesus did not die so that we could become better at hiding our sins beneath religious language.
He died to redeem sinners and make them new.
That includes the person who was wounded.
And it includes the person who did the wounding.
Perhaps that person is you.
Perhaps you were a parent who spoke words your child still hears in their mind.
Perhaps you were a husband who dismissed your wife's tears until she stopped trying to explain them.
Perhaps you were a wife who used your husband's vulnerabilities as weapons during an argument.
Perhaps you were a friend who exposed a secret entrusted to you.
Perhaps you were a church leader who confused spiritual authority with the right to control or humiliate people.
Perhaps you were a son or daughter who spoke cruelly to a parent.
Perhaps you were a believer who publicly shamed another believer and privately justified it as defending the truth.
Or perhaps you wounded someone through neglect.
You didn't scream.
You didn't threaten.
You simply disappeared when they needed you.
You broke a promise.
You betrayed their trust.
You let them carry a burden that should never have been theirs alone.
And now, every time the memory returns, you push it away.
Because remembering would mean facing it.
And facing it might mean apologizing.
But there is something more frightening than admitting you were wrong.
It is spending years protecting your pride while your heart becomes increasingly resistant to the voice of God.
The apostle John wrote:
"If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?" (1 John 4:20, KJV)
John's language is devastatingly clear.
In the Greek text, the word for love is connected to ἀγαπάω (agapaō), the verb used in this passage to describe love for God and love for one's brother.
Biblical love is not merely an emotion we claim to possess.
It must be expressed in how we live.
Now, this passage does not mean that every person struggling to apologize necessarily hates someone or has never truly loved God.
That would go beyond what John says.
But it does confront the contradiction of claiming devotion to God while deliberately nurturing hatred toward others.
And if we claim to love God while repeatedly refusing to acknowledge the harm we knowingly cause, we have reason to examine our hearts.
Not because apologizing earns salvation.
It does not.
But because a heart being transformed by Christ should become increasingly willing to confess sin, pursue peace, and practice humility.
The evidence of grace is not perfection.
It is a life being changed.
And genuine change cannot remain forever trapped in beautiful words.
Eventually, it must reach the people affected by our behavior.
This is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us are waiting for the people we hurt to apologize first.
We keep a mental record.
Who started it.
Who said what.
Who was more disrespectful.
Who caused the greater damage.
We rehearse their failures so thoroughly that we no longer have to examine our own.
But repentance is not a competition over who committed the greater offense.
You can be genuinely hurt by someone and still need to repent for the way you responded.
You can have been mistreated and still be responsible for your own sinful choices.
Two people can both need to apologize.
And one person's refusal to repent does not make the other person's wrongdoing righteous.
Romans 12:18 says:
"If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men." (KJV)
Those opening words matter.
"If it be possible."
God does not command you to manufacture reconciliation where another person refuses it.
He does not command you to return to an abusive relationship.
He does not require victims to surrender necessary boundaries, expose themselves to danger, or restore trust without evidence of change.
Forgiveness, repentance, reconciliation, and restored trust are related, but they are not identical.
An apology does not automatically restore access.
Forgiveness does not erase consequences.
Reconciliation ordinarily requires more than one person's participation.
And where abuse, coercion, or serious harm has occurred, genuine repentance includes respecting boundaries, accepting accountability, and allowing the harmed person to seek safety and justice.
Sometimes the wisest apology is made through a safe intermediary.
Sometimes direct contact would cause additional harm.
Sometimes the person you hurt is no longer alive.
Sometimes they have made it clear they do not want to hear from you.
In those situations, repentance is not measured by forcing an unwanted conversation.
It is measured by truthful confession, appropriate restitution where possible, changed conduct, and respect for the other person's well-being.
God is not honored when we use reconciliation as a spiritual excuse to violate someone's boundaries.
But neither is He honored when we use the language of boundaries to conceal our refusal to take responsibility.
And perhaps this is the question that matters most.
If the person you hurt never apologizes to you, are you still willing to take responsibility for what you did?
That question reaches deeper than pride.
It reaches into the heart of the Gospel.
Because when we look at Jesus Christ, we encounter a Savior whose humility exposes our obsession with defending ourselves.
Philippians 2:5–8 calls believers to have the mind of Christ, describing how Jesus humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
The Greek word ἐταπείνωσεν (etapeinōsen) in Philippians 2:8 means "he humbled."
Jesus willingly humbled Himself.
Not because He had sinned.
He was sinless.
Not because He owed an apology.
He owed none.
But because His obedience to the Father led Him along the path of self-giving love.
And here is the contrast we must face.
The sinless Savior humbled Himself to save sinners.
Yet sometimes we, the sinners He came to save, refuse to humble ourselves enough to admit that we wounded another human being.
We want to follow the crucified Christ.
But we don't want our pride crucified.
We want resurrection power.
But we resist the death of self-exaltation.
We want God to forgive our offenses.
But we become offended at the suggestion that we should acknowledge them.
And still...
Jesus calls us closer.
Not to crush us with condemnation.
But to bring us into the freedom of truth.
There is a difference between conviction and hopelessness.
Conviction says, "What you did was wrong. Bring it into the light."
Hopelessness says, "What you did is all you will ever be."
The Gospel rejects that hopelessness.
Consider Peter.
He boldly declared his loyalty to Jesus.
Then, on the night of Jesus' arrest, he denied knowing Him three times.
The Gospel of Luke records that after Peter's denial, the Lord turned and looked at him.
Peter remembered Jesus' words.
And he went out and wept bitterly.
Imagine that moment.
The sound of the rooster.
The memory of his promises.
The weight of his failure.
The realization that the man who said he would never abandon Jesus had denied Him.
Peter could not undo those words.
He could not rewind that night.
He could not make the failure disappear.
But failure was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, in John 21, Jesus met Peter and asked him three times about his love.
Jesus also entrusted him with the responsibility to care for His sheep.

The passage is not a simplistic formula for every broken relationship, and its Greek vocabulary should not be forced into an unsupported distinction between supposedly superior and inferior kinds of love.
But the scene unmistakably reveals something beautiful.
Jesus did not treat Peter's failure as the final chapter of his life.
He confronted Peter's love and restored him to service.
The same Christ who knew Peter's denial also knew what grace could make of him.
And maybe someone reading this needs to hear that.
Your worst moment does not have to become your permanent identity.
Your pride does not have to win.
Your past does not have to dictate your future.
But grace is not permission to continue the very behavior from which Christ calls you to turn.
Grace brings us to repentance.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains us to deny ungodliness and live in a way that honors Him.
Grace is not merely pardon from sin's guilt.
It also teaches us to leave sin behind.
So when someone says, "I already asked God to forgive me," we must ask a further question.
Has that forgiveness led you toward repentance?
Because confession to God should not become a substitute for making things right with people when doing so is possible and appropriate.
Look at Zacchaeus.
In Luke 19, this wealthy chief tax collector encountered Jesus.
And something changed.
Zacchaeus declared that he would give half his goods to the poor and restore fourfold what he had wrongfully taken.
He did not merely announce that he was now a better man.
He demonstrated a willingness to address the harm he had caused.
Jesus responded by declaring that salvation had come to his house.
Zacchaeus did not purchase salvation through restitution.
His response showed the transforming impact of encountering Christ.
This matters.
Because sometimes an apology without changed behavior is simply another way of asking the wounded person to carry the cost of our choices.
"I'm sorry" matters.
But so does what happens afterward.
If you lied, begin telling the truth.
If you stole, make appropriate restitution.
If you slandered someone publicly, consider whether your correction also needs to be public.
If you repeatedly broke promises, stop demanding immediate trust and begin demonstrating reliability.
If you manipulated someone, stop trying to control how they respond to your repentance.
If you harmed someone seriously, accept the appropriate consequences.
And if you apologize, do not turn the apology into another accusation.
"I'm sorry you felt hurt" is not the same as acknowledging what you did.
"I'm sorry, but you made me angry" is not full ownership.
"I'm sorry, so can we just forget everything?" may place pressure on someone who is still healing.
Sometimes the most Christ-honoring words are simple.
"I was wrong."
"What I said was cruel."
"I betrayed your trust."
"You did not deserve that."
"I am sorry for what I did."
"I understand that forgiveness may take time."
"I want to change, whether or not you are ready to reconcile."
No performance.
No bargaining.
No demand for immediate absolution.
Just truth.
Humility.
Responsibility.
And a willingness to let genuine repentance produce visible fruit.
Second Corinthians 7:10 says:
"For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death." (KJV)
The Greek expression μετάνοια (metanoia) refers to repentance, a turning of mind and life.
In this context, Paul distinguishes godly sorrow, which produces repentance, from worldly sorrow, which leads toward death.
There is a kind of regret that is mostly concerned with consequences.
Regret over being exposed.
Regret over losing someone's admiration.
Regret over the damage to our reputation.
Regret that someone now sees us differently.
But godly sorrow moves beyond the fear of consequences.
It recognizes the wrong itself.
It seeks to turn away from it.
It takes seriously both the holiness of God and the dignity of the person who was harmed.
That is the difference between saying, "I'm sorry you found out," and saying, "I'm sorry I sinned against you."
And perhaps one of the hardest truths to accept is that sincere repentance does not entitle us to a particular response.
The person may forgive you.
They may need time.
They may choose not to resume the relationship.
They may never trust you in the same way again.
Your apology cannot become another means of controlling them.
Your responsibility is to repent sincerely and do what is right before God.
Their response belongs to them.
That is a painful surrender.
Especially when you desperately want the story to end with an embrace.
But not every earthly relationship ends with reconciliation.
Some stories end with an apology that is never answered.
Some end with distance.
Some end with consequences that remain even after genuine repentance.
And yet God's grace can still be at work.
Because redemption does not always mean getting back everything you lost.
Sometimes redemption means becoming the kind of person who will never again treat someone the way you once did.
Sometimes it means finally telling the truth.
Sometimes it means accepting a consequence without bitterness.
Sometimes it means loving someone enough to respect the distance they need.
And sometimes it means sitting alone before God, with tears on your face, and admitting something you have spent years trying not to say.
"Lord, I was the one who hurt them."
Not because every accusation against you is true.
Not because every conflict is entirely your fault.
But because you have finally stopped hiding the part that is yours.
Psalm 51 records David's repentance after his grievous sin.
He cried:
"Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me." (Psalm 51:10, KJV)
In Hebrew, the expression לֵב טָהוֹר (lev tahor) means "a clean heart."
And בְּרָא־לִי (bera-li) expresses the plea, "create for me."
David was asking God for something deeper than a repaired reputation.
He needed inward renewal.
Yet David's story also reminds us that repentance does not erase earthly consequences.
His wrongdoing was serious.
His confession did not make the suffering he caused insignificant.
And this is important because Christian language about grace must never be used to minimize victims or protect perpetrators from accountability.
The God who forgives sinners is also the God who loves righteousness and justice.
You cannot use the blood of Jesus as an excuse to keep hurting people.
You cannot demand that someone trust you simply because you say you have repented.
You cannot claim spiritual maturity while refusing the ordinary work of humility, truthfulness, and restitution.
And you cannot make your religious activities a substitute for obedience.
But there is hope.
There is so much hope.
Because the same Jesus who confronts our sin also welcomes repentant sinners.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
Notice what God promises.
Forgiveness.
Cleansing.
Not a license to hide.
Not a guarantee that everyone will reconcile with us.
But real mercy for those who come to Him in truth.
And if you are reading this with a memory pressing against your heart, perhaps this is your moment to stop running.
Maybe there is a message you need to send.
Maybe there is a conversation you need to approach with humility.
Maybe you need to confess something to a trusted pastor, counselor, or mature believer who can help you pursue repentance responsibly.
Maybe you need to make restitution.
Maybe you need to stop making excuses for your temper.
Maybe you need to acknowledge that your children were hurt by the words you spoke over them.
Maybe you need to admit that being a respected Christian in public does not excuse being cruel in private.
And maybe you need to hear this, too.
If you are the person who was hurt, this article is not permission for anyone to pressure you into unsafe reconciliation.
Your pain matters.
Your safety matters.
The truth matters.
You are not required to pretend that an apology automatically repairs the damage.
You are not obligated to make someone feel better about their wrongdoing by rushing your healing.
Jesus sees you too.
He sees the tears that never became public testimony.
He sees the prayers you whispered when nobody else believed you.
He sees the confusion of loving someone who repeatedly wounded you.
And He does not ask you to call evil good.
He calls His people to walk in truth.
Perhaps that is why this message is so difficult.
It leaves none of us with a comfortable hiding place.
Those who caused harm must face responsibility.
Those who have been harmed must not be silenced or coerced.
Those who are angry must guard against becoming consumed by hatred.
Those who are proud must learn humility.
And every one of us must come before the cross as someone who needs the mercy of Jesus Christ.
Not merely as a teacher of morality.
Not merely as an example of kindness.
But as the crucified and risen Savior.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we perfected our behavior.
Not after we earned divine approval.
Not after we repaired every relationship.
Christ died for sinners.
And His resurrection is the foundation of our living hope.
This is why repentance is possible without despair.
We can admit our sins because we do not have to pretend that we are our own saviors.
We can surrender our pride because our identity does not have to rest on always being right.
We can confess the truth because the Gospel announces that forgiveness is found in Jesus Christ.
And we can begin changing because the Holy Spirit is at work in those who belong to Him.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
It does not flatter us.
It tells the truth about our sin.
But it does not abandon us in our sin.
It points us to the Savior.
And the Savior calls us to follow Him.
Not only in church.
Not only when the music is playing.
Not only when we are posting inspirational words.
But in the uncomfortable conversations.
In the family wounds.
In the broken friendships.
In the marriages where pride has become a wall.
In the private moments when nobody is watching.
In the decision to apologize even when it costs us our image of being the innocent one.
Because the question was never simply whether you can pronounce the words "I love God."
The question is whether that love is changing the way you live.
And no, one unresolved apology does not automatically prove that you have never loved God.
Christians still struggle with fear, shame, confusion, and pride.
But persistent, deliberate refusal to repent of known wrongdoing is spiritually serious.
It should move us toward honest self-examination rather than comfortable self-assurance.
Jesus said:
"If ye love me, keep my commandments." (John 14:15, KJV)
Obedience does not purchase His love.
It is a response to His love.
And when His Word exposes our pride, the faithful response is not to silence our conscience.
It is to come to Him.
Perhaps tonight, instead of asking God to change the person who hurt you, you may need to ask Him whether there is someone you have hurt.
Perhaps both prayers are necessary.
Perhaps the relationship cannot be repaired.
Perhaps the person is gone.
Perhaps you will never have the opportunity to say everything you wish you had said.
Even then, you can repent.
You can seek God's forgiveness.
You can make amends where possible.
You can become more truthful, more humble, more patient, and more careful with the hearts entrusted to you.
You can allow Christ to transform how you treat the next person.
And if you still have the opportunity to apologize safely and appropriately, do not assume that tomorrow is guaranteed.
There may be a person who has waited years to hear you acknowledge the truth.
Not to win.
Not to humiliate you.
Not to destroy your faith.
But simply to know that their pain was real to you.
Imagine what it would mean for a grown child to hear a parent say:
"I should never have spoken to you that way."
Imagine what it would mean for a spouse to hear:
"I made you feel alone when I should have listened."
Imagine what it would mean for a friend to hear:
"You trusted me, and I betrayed that trust."
Imagine what it would mean for someone wounded by a Christian to hear:
"What I did was wrong. Please don't confuse my behavior with the character of Jesus."
An apology may not heal everything.
It may not restore the relationship.
But sincere acknowledgment can matter profoundly.
And even where reconciliation is impossible, obedience to God is never wasted.
So here is the question I want you to carry after this article ends.
Are you asking God to heal a relationship while refusing to confront the behavior that helped break it?
Do not answer too quickly.
Let the Word of God examine you.
Let the Holy Spirit bring conviction where conviction is needed.
Let the grace of Christ give you courage to confess.
And let repentance become something more than a religious word.
Make it visible.
Make it truthful.
Make it costly when it needs to be.
Not to earn God's mercy.
But because you have received mercy you could never earn.
If this message has exposed something in your heart, you do not need to tell the whole internet the details of your private situation. But you are welcome to take one honest step into the light.
Not because a comment proves your faith.
Not because public confession is required for forgiveness.
But because sometimes a simple, honest testimony reminds another struggling believer that they are not walking alone.
There may be someone reading the comments who needs to know that grace is still available, that repentance is still possible, and that healing does not have to be rushed.
And if someone came to mind while you were reading, consider sharing this article with them—not as a weapon, not as a public accusation, but as an invitation to reflect on what Jesus teaches.
Not because Gospel Warrior has all the answers.
But because we want to keep pointing people to the One who does.
Jesus Christ.
His Word.
His cross.
His resurrection.
His grace.
His call to repentance.
And His power to transform lives.
Gospel Warrior is working to build a place where believers can continue growing in biblical understanding, spiritual maturity, and daily discipleship.
We want biblical nourishment to remain accessible.
We want wounded people to encounter the hope of the Gospel.
We want those wrestling with sin to hear both the seriousness of repentance and the beauty of God's mercy.
We want families strengthened, believers equipped, and the name of Jesus Christ proclaimed faithfully.
And this work requires time, resources, and people who believe it is worth sustaining.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
But an opportunity to support Gospel-centered work if you believe in the mission and have the means to participate.
These are tangible ways to enjoy and share faith-centered resources while helping sustain the work.
Read.
Grow.
Pray.
Invite others.
Use the free resources.
Someone who needs to apologize.
Someone who needs to hear that repentance is possible.
Someone who has confused religious activity with genuine surrender.
Someone who has been hurt by a professing Christian and needs to see that Jesus does not excuse cruelty.
Someone who has spent years believing their worst mistake placed them beyond redemption.
If Gospel Warrior can help even one more person open the Scriptures, confront sin honestly, and turn toward Jesus Christ, that is a reason to keep laboring faithfully.
And before you leave, I want to pray with you.
Father in heaven,
Search our hearts.
Not only the parts we show people.
Not only the parts that look spiritual.
But the places where pride has become comfortable.
Forgive us for the times we have used religious words to escape personal responsibility.
Forgive us for the pain we have caused through anger, selfishness, dishonesty, neglect, and arrogance.
Give us courage to acknowledge the truth without excuses.
Give us humility to apologize where we have done wrong.
Give us wisdom to pursue reconciliation without causing further harm.
Teach us to respect the boundaries of those we have wounded.
And for those carrying the pain of an apology that never came, draw near to them with Your compassion.
Protect them from despair.
Give them wise support, peace, and strength.
Help them understand that another person's refusal to repent does not determine their worth.
Lord Jesus, thank You for bearing our sins on the cross.
Thank You that Your resurrection declares the victory of our Savior over death.
Thank You that Your grace is greater than our ability to repair ourselves.
Create in us clean hearts.
Make our repentance sincere.
Make our love visible.
Teach us to walk in truth.
And let our lives testify not merely that we know Christian words, but that we belong to Jesus Christ.
In His holy name,
Amen.
And now, one final thought.
There may come a day when you no longer have the opportunity to speak to the person you hurt.
A day when the phone number no longer works.
When the chair is empty.
When the door has closed.
When the conversation you kept postponing is no longer possible.
None of us knows how much time we have.
So do not waste the opportunities God gives you to pursue truth, humility, and peace.
You do not have to win every argument.
You do not have to defend every mistake.
You do not have to remain the person you were when you caused the wound.
Because Jesus Christ is able to change a human heart.
And the Gospel does not end with the exposure of sin.
It leads repentant sinners to the grace of the crucified and risen Savior.
One day, the words you refused to say may become the words you wish you had spoken while there was still time.
